title: Renormalization-group locking of finite anisotropic propagation cones in Yukawa networks
abstract: Different field species can begin with finite anisotropic propagation geometries whose principal axes need not coincide. We ask whether local Yukawa interactions on a finite graph can nevertheless generate one common infrared spatial cone, even when the interactions that drive the locking become marginally irrelevant. Retaining the full finite mismatch between positive-definite spatial kinetic matrices, we derive the one-loop nonlinear matrix flow and show that its Thompson diameter is globally nonexpansive. On a connected graph, persistent normalized edge activity upgrades this to a uniform finite-window contraction, so all interacting sectors asymptotically share one relative propagation geometry. An explicit two-channel Pauli-Dirac Yukawa-quartic completion realizes the persistence conditions on an open weak-coupling set of finite-mismatch initial data. In four dimensions the Yukawa couplings vanish in the infrared, yet their accumulated interaction time diverges, leaving a Gaussian endpoint with a common spatial cone. For a controlled two-plateau extremal class, graph distance also fixes the first nonzero short-time order of the diameter decrease. Thus a common cone can be collectively selected by renormalization-group dynamics rather than imposed as a microscopic common structure.
summary: This theoretical paper analyzes how local Yukawa interactions on a network can force disparate physical fields into sharing a single common infrared propagation cone. By deriving nonlinear matrix flow equations, the authors prove that renormalization group dynamics drive this geometric locking across the entire connected system. This demonstrates that global structure can emerge from local interactions via RG evolution.
main_problem: The study investigates whether local Yukawa interactions on a finite graph can force different field species to share a single common infrared spatial propagation cone, even when the interactions driving this locking are marginally irrelevant.
main_result: Renormalization-group dynamics can collectively select and enforce a common relative propagation geometry (common-cone locking) across all interacting sectors in the network.
method: The analysis involves deriving one-loop nonlinear matrix flow equations for the kinetic matrices, utilizing concepts from differential geometry like the Thompson diameter to quantify geometric mismatch.
model_or_system: The model is a multichannel Dirac–scalar Yukawa theory defined on a finite bipartite graph. Fields possess anisotropic propagation geometries described by positive-definite spatial kinetic matrices.
key_observables: Thompson diameter (DT), which quantifies the mismatch in relative propagation geometry; the evolution of the relative matrix R.
important_parameters: One-loop approximation, weak coupling regime, finite graph connectivity, and graph distance controlling onset order.
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes positive-definite spatial kinetic matrices and requires persistent normalized edge activity to achieve full contraction.
figures_summary: Figures conceptually illustrate the transition from initial anisotropic cones to a common-cone locked state driven by RG flow, with connectivity determining the asymptotic fate.
paper_structure: The paper develops the one-loop nonlinear matrix flow equations for relative kinetic matrices. It proves that this flow leads to global nonexpansion and, under persistent activity, a finite-window contraction of the Thompson diameter, demonstrating common-cone locking.
why_interesting: While focused on field theory, the use of RG flow dynamics, geometric invariants (Thompson diameter), and convergence proofs for coupled systems provides powerful mathematical tools applicable to analyzing complex many-body relaxation or synchronization in quantum systems.

figures.caption: Figure 1. Conceptual overview of common-cone locking in a connected Yukawa network. Left: fermion and scalar nodes carry node-dependent anisotropic spatial propagation cones. Middle: the one-loop RG acts on the connected bipartite interaction graph. Right: persistent connected interactions drive relative common-cone locking, quantified by DT →0. Connectivity underlies the global-locking theorem, while graph distance controls the onset order in the topology-sensitive short-time law.

Figure 2. Representative locking trajectories of the normalized finite-matrix flow. (a) Thompson diameter DT for the same four initial SPD cones on the path P4 and the complete bipartite graph K2,2, with bαe = bβe = 1. (b) Normalized diameter for sixteen random connected 2 + 3 bipartite networks with positive rates in the interval eq. (4.28); the black curve is the pointwise median. The horizontal variable s is accumulated interaction time.

Figure 3. Topology-sensitive onset for symmetric two-plateau data on path graphs. (a) Diameter decrease DT (0) −DT (s) for P4, P6, P8, together with the predicted sq scaling; the parenthetical values in the legend are fitted powers over eq. (5.21). (b) Effective exponent qeff(s), approaching 2, 3, 4 toward short accumulated interaction time.
